notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0104p.stoa006.opp-l: Scanning errors read as evident: 'm homine' as 'in homine', 'fontom' as 'fontem', 'nino corpore' as 'uiuo corpore' (living body), 'modum' as 'modo' (just now). In 5.1 the punctuation before 'super haec' is missing; read as a new sentence. 'Aquas contradictionis' is the Vulgate's rendering of the waters of Meribah.

Evident scanning errors read as: 'ant' = aut; 'nonum testamentum' = novum; 'oboritnr' = oboritur; 'dom' = dum. In the Colossians quotations the text has 'pro nobis' and 'in nobis' where Col 1:24-25 reads 'pro vobis', 'in vos/vobis'; translated as 'for you', taking these as misreadings. The edition's punctuation 'quasi sit una. passio Domini et seruorum. id. ne quia' is garbled; read as 'quasi sit una passio Domini et servorum. Id ne quis existimet...'. 'replevisse evangelium' (Rom 15:19) rendered 'fully preached / fill out the gospel'.

Scanning errors read as evident: 'ui uere' = uiuere, 'carificinae' = carnificinae, 'neri' = ueri, 'uiuimu$' = uiuimus, 'ludam' = Iudam, 'summum ... stultitiam' = summam. In 16.1 (ref 14.1) 'prolixe atque etiam frequenter' lacks a verb; a word such as 'orans' seems to have dropped out, supplied as [praying]. 'faciet ... cum tentatione prouentum' rendered 'make a way out' (1 Cor 10:13).

19.1: 'disponsator' read as 'dispensator' (steward). 21.1: 'apud uos' ('among you') translated as 'apud nos' ('among us'), which the sense requires; 'xara' is the Greek κατά ('according to'); 'enangelii' read as 'euangelii'. 24.1: 'anaritia' read as 'auaritia'; 'malamao' read as 'malam' (Col 3:5 'concupiscentiam malam'). 24.1: the remark that Paul 'said sentire for colere' does not fit the quotation as printed, which has 'seruiunt'; the text may be corrupt here, or the author may be working from a variant reading of Rom 16:18. 24.1: 'cur et nobis adeo blandimur et aliis' seems elliptical, and is translated as it stands.

26.1: 'turificatus' and 'libellatus' are the Decian-era terms for lapsed Christians who sacrificed incense or bought certificates of sacrifice. 27.1: 'ad Turcam' is an anachronism in a text ascribed to Cyprian, consistent with Erasmus' authorship. 27.1 end: the text reads 'Christum lingua aut habitu Christum profitearis', apparently with a concessive word (e.g. 'licet') lost; translated as 'even if'. 28.1: the sentence about the Maccabees is punctuated in the edition with a full stop after 'negare'; read as continuous ('negare quisquis... violat'). 29.1: 'disperdet illam' in the quotation presumably for 'illum'; rendered 'him'. 'Como' taken as Comus, god of revelry.

30.1: the text reads 'nolenti' ('not wishing'); the sense and 2 Tim 3:12 require 'uolenti' ('wishing'), which is translated. 33.1: 'ceuangelium euangelium')' is a scanning garble of 'euangelium'; 'iusultant' read as 'insultant', 'nonum' as 'nouum'. 36.1: the last clause 'qui in prauo positus est' is read as echoing 1 John 5:19 ('the world lies in wickedness'), referring to the world; it could instead refer to the man ('who is set in wickedness').
Line 37: 'Eihmci putant plurea' read as 'Ethnici putant plures'. Line 38: 'lacessitus ea conuicio' read as 'lacessitus es conuicio'; 'in a dies' read as 'in dies'.

nodes.text: XIV. ON THE TWOFOLD MARTYRDOM, TO FORTUNATUS.

In many ways and by many means I give thanks, Fortunatus, dearest to me in the Lord, to the divine kindness: first, that it stirred up your devotion to spur on my duty, so that in a single small book I might supply our fellow soldiers with material from which, with the grace of the Spirit helping, they could forge for themselves defences and weapons against the onslaughts of persecution, and that it did not disdain to be present with me as I attempted what you asked; and further, that it did not allow the labour of either of us to be barren, that is, that it made the pious desire of my Fortunatus turn out fortunately, and willed the service of its minister to be a benefit to its flock. For you write that from that book much strength and eagerness has come to the vigorous, while to the more timid and the weak so much courage has been added that from them too, through the grace of God, we ought to promise ourselves a sure victory. And so all the more gladly have I complied with your later letter, in which your charity asks that, since this has turned out well under the auspices of our Lord Jesus Christ, I add a second volume on the twofold kind of martyrdom: of which one is displayed when the savagery of the torturers rages, while the other is indeed more hidden, but nonetheless demands a brave mind, well fortified with much armour from God. May the Spirit of Christ deign to bestow this gift too through me on our brothers and fellow soldiers, and to prosper well what he gives. For just as nothing is holy unless he sanctifies it, nothing powerful unless he strengthens it, so nothing is happy, nothing well-omened, unless he prospers it. Relying, then, both on your prayers and on the goodness of the Lord, I shall set about it.
"Martyr", as is known even to those who do not know Greek, means "witness".

But although, after the light of the gospel truth arose, the custom of the Church assigned the honour of this title properly to those who persevered under torture even to death in confessing the name of Jesus Christ, and as it were sealed the gospel record with their blood before unbelievers, yet the whole life of the godly bears witness to God. Not that he needs anyone's witness, he who is of himself the source of eternal glory, so that he can neither be made more honoured by any human honours nor more obscure by any disgraces from mortals; but nevertheless it has so seemed good to his eternal and divine counsel that he wills his goodness, wisdom and power to be made illustrious among men through men, just as he willed the world to be governed through angels, though he has no need of the ministry of angels, and bestows many things on men through men which he could give by himself, he who can do whatever he wills with a nod, and for whom to have willed is to have done. And although, as I said, no disgrace reaches that ineffable majesty, yet in the scriptures he speaks as if he were honoured or dishonoured through us. For in Deuteronomy he remonstrates with Moses because, among the people murmuring for lack of water at Kadesh in the desert of Zin, at the waters of contradiction, he did not sanctify him among the sons of Israel; and for this offence it was not granted to him, nor to Aaron, to enter the promised land, awaited for so many years, but he was only permitted to view it from afar from the top of a mountain.

Further, that "sanctify" is said for "glorify", those skilled in Hebrew letters affirm is an idiom of that language. Yet this itself can be clear from other places of the scriptures, if we have less trust in their testimony, since in the Lord's Prayer too "hallowed be your name" is said for "glorified" or "made bright be your name". So too he exhorts the Corinthians to glorify and bear God in their body. For just as the name of God is glorified by the life of godly men, in whom he himself through his Spirit works whatever good they do, so conversely it is polluted and defamed by the misdeeds of those who profess themselves worshippers of God. And just as the courage of a soldier or the honesty of a slave redounds to the glory of the commander or the master, so the cowardice of a soldier or the wickedness of a slave is a disgrace to the commander or master, because the conduct of the former depends in great part on the conduct of those in whose power they are. And even if these are wholly free of all blame, yet popular opinion usually judges the conduct of masters from the conduct of slaves. Hence here too we see divine scripture often speaking according to the feelings of mortals, as in Leviticus it says of one who had given of his seed to the idol Molech: "because he has polluted my holy name". But what is sanctified by men can be polluted; the name of God, however, is always glorious in itself, and is defiled only among men, just as lying infamy does not pollute an upright man. So too in Ezekiel he cries out that his name had been polluted among the nations by the impious conduct of the Israelites. Indeed the most blessed Paul too, writing to the Romans, on the authority of the prophet says, addressing the Jews who professed the law but did what the law forbids: "The name of God is blasphemed among the nations." And in the Lord's Prayer, as I touched on just now, on the authority of the Redeemer we pray that the name of God the Father be hallowed, that is, that it become bright and illustrious among men, certainly through men, or rather in men. And it is made illustrious if his Spirit reigns in us and if his will is obeyed on earth, as in heaven there is no rebellion. But since men have of themselves no power, whatever is done rightly through us redounds to the glory of God; and for this reason he sometimes brings out the treasure of divine power from earthen vessels, so that the sublimity of the power may be God's and not from us.

Therefore, although the whole life of the godly glorifies God and Christ his Son by its witness, yet no witness among men is more illustrious than that of blood, that is, of life despised for God's sake and of death bravely endured. Miracles too have borne witness to the divine power, especially among unbelievers, for signs were given properly to them, as the blessed apostle writes; but the witness of shed blood has always been more effective. How many incurable diseases had the Lord healed by a word, how many blind had he given light, how many maimed, paralysed and infirm had he restored, how many lifeless had he called back to life? And yet few believed in him, and he heard: "By Beelzebub he has cast out demons." But when it came to blood, there Satan's kingdom was thrown down, there the world was subdued. John the evangelist too records a threefold witness on earth, the spirit, the water and the blood, listing in last place the one that is most effective. The Spirit descending on Jesus in the form of a dove John the Baptist was found worthy to see; whether others saw it is uncertain. Certainly this witness was given to John, so that he might cease to doubt about the Lord Jesus, whether he was the one who would baptise with the Spirit and fire. The witness of the water John the evangelist saw, and it is not quite clear whether he saw it alone or with many. This was indeed the great mystery of the sacred washing by which sins are blotted out; but he saw water flowing out together with blood, and had the blood not been present the water would have been ineffective. For what does it profit for sins to be abolished unless there follows the life of righteousness which the blood confers? Yet these three are one: for there is one God, who through spirit, water and blood declares his power and goodness to the human race; or else they are said to be one because the witness is consistent on every side and in no part out of harmony, just as those whom the closest friendship joins are said to be one soul because of the supreme agreement of their minds.

And according to a more physical sense, these three are the chief signs, and also instruments, of life in a man. For as long as breath is drawn in and given back in turn by the work of the lungs, it is a sure indication of life; hence in common speech those who live are said to breathe, and those who have ended life to have breathed out. Indeed, the soul too is called by the Latins anima, "breath", in imitation of the Greek word, for they call wind anemos. Besides these there are in man himself most subtle spirits, spread from the heart, where they have their source, through the whole body, but travelling chiefly through the arteries, though mixed also with all the other parts: if these fly out suddenly they bring instant death; but if they are shut in, they consume a man with a slow illness. There is also a certain natural moisture, which, as I think, physicians call phlegm, itself also spread through the whole body. We never feel its use more evidently than in the sense of taste: for unless it is mixed in between tongue and palate, the palate will have no judgement. And yet these are so mixed in man that there is no blood without spirit and phlegm, and all alike contribute to preserving life. We see that any animal dies as soon as its blood has flowed out; and when the moisture which physicians call radical is used up, a man dies no otherwise than a lamp goes out when the oil is used up. But we are lingering too long in the contemplation of nature; yet I think this has not been done uselessly by us, so that the mystery may become clearer to your charity, a mystery in whose contemplation we occupy ourselves the more gladly because the more wholesomely. For according to the consideration of nature these things have great force when they perform their functions in a living body; but according to mystical philosophy they are most powerful precisely when they leave the body.

No one wondered at the Lord breathing in and breathing out in human fashion; but when on the cross he had sent forth his spirit with a loud cry, it was understood at once that he was both true man and true God: man, because according to the order of nature, when he had sent forth the vital breath, he ceased to live; God, because he died with a mighty cry, declaring that he laid down his life unforced and of his own will, which no one is unaware is not within human strength. The centurion standing nearby perceived the effective witness of the spirit, for so blessed Mark tells it: "And when the centurion who stood facing him saw that he had expired thus, he said: Truly this man was the Son of God." What is more abject than death according to the flesh? But nothing is more powerful than death according to the spirit. This too was beyond the course of nature, that from the side of the lifeless body blood and water flowed out, so that the threefold witness might be completed. He poured out all his spirit so that we might breathe again; whatever moisture of water remained, he pressed out so that we might be washed; whatever blood had settled in the heart, he sent forth so that we might be strengthened. And I do not know whether I am wrong to compare these three with one another, since they are one not by nature but in mystery. Yet if there is any distinction, blood is most celebrated in the account of the witnesses, because Scripture testifies that in it is the life of a living creature, and for that reason it was excluded from food by the edict of the law; moreover blood is more exposed to men's eyes than spirit or water.

The life of the Lord, who was the supreme martyr and who today too fights and conquers in the martyrs, was a stumbling block to very many. I do not now speak of the Pharisees and scribes; even to his own kinsmen and brothers he was detestable, since they said he had gone mad. But his death was wonderful not only to the pious but even to the impious, and nowhere was it more true that the power of God is made perfect in weakness. There the tyranny of Satan was broken, there the underworld was conquered, there triumph was won over the devil, there hell was cast down and heaven opened. Surely this was what the Lord prayed for as the time of death drew near: "Father, glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you." What is more contemptible than a dead man? For who would fear even a dead Caesar? But what is more effective than the death of Christ? The veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom, the earth was shaken, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, the bodies of the buried came back to life, the sun covered its face at midday. Never in his whole life did he show his power more; soon, having broken all the bars of death, he showed himself alive to his disciples. Surely this is that effective witness of the most holy blood, which alone could break down the wall that separated God from the human race; it alone could with a single stroke blot out that whole bond which was against us and claimed for Satan his right over us. For the blood of goats or calves could not abolish sin: those were shadows and types of things to come. Nor could the blood of any man take away the sin of the world, except the blood of that only Lamb, to whom the Baptist bore witness, saying: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world."

It is more to take away sin than sins, and sin not of this man or that but of the world. For the body of sin had taken possession of the whole world: that this has been taken away through Christ his blood shed for us gives clear witness, speaking better for us, as the apostle says, than the blood of Abel. For that blood, crying from the earth, spoke vengeance; but the blood of Christ, crying from the cross, speaks peace and reconciliation. Indeed the same blood, since it is drunk by us, provided only it is drunk worthily, cries in our hearts words of peace and full of comfort. And there too the witness is threefold, though in a certain spiritual manner. The Spirit, who has been given to us as a pledge, cries: "Abba, Father," testifying that we are sons of God. The water through which we have been reborn cries that all our sins have been forgiven us; and if anyone still doubts, there is added the witness of the blood, crying: "Why do you still hesitate, why do you still dread the tyrant Satan? Behold the price with which the Son of God redeems you. Had God not willed you saved, he would not have handed over his only-begotten to death."

"No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his life for his friends." If there is no greater witness of exceptional goodwill than when someone gives his life for a friend, weightier is the witness of the Lord's blood, which was shed for enemies. Shed for enemies, it made them friends and sons of God; and so that we might consider that this friendship would be perpetual, he left us his flesh to eat, he left his blood to drink, so that we might be nourished by the same things by which we were redeemed. By the sprinkling of blood the old testament was confirmed, as the most blessed Paul, writing to the Hebrews, excellently teaches; by the blood of Christ the new testament was sealed and strengthened, that is, the testament and covenant of grace and of the remission of sins through the blood of the spotless Lamb, who deigned to take upon himself the sin of the whole world, which all who come forth into this life contract from Adam, and by whose contagion all who sin, sin. But so great is the sublimity of Christ that perhaps no one of other men ought to be compared with him, had he not himself given us such confidence, he who did not disdain to call his disciples friends, and his poor servants brothers and co-heirs. Just as, then, he by his wonderful witness glorified the Father in this world and also in the heavens, so his witness is in a way completed by the witness of the saints, as though the passion of the Lord and of his servants were one. Lest anyone think this said with too little reverence, blessed Paul defends us, writing thus to the Colossians: "I who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ, for his body, which is the church." For who does not know, brothers, what a rich harvest the crop of the church has poured forth, watered by the blood of the apostles and the other martyrs? The more blood was shed, the more the multitude of the faithful flourished, the more widely that blessed vine, rising from Christ as its stock, spread its shoots, taking possession of the whole world wherever it extends from east to west, from north to south.

See, dearest brothers, from the times of the Lord the Redeemer about two hundred and forty years have passed, and already the branches of this vine have spread almost more widely than the Roman empire, intoxicating even savage nations with the new wine of the Spirit; and those whom no force of iron could tame, the blood of that white Lamb softens. Those who investigate the causes of nature relate that adamant, which yields to no hardness of steel, when steeped in goat's blood shatters under the blows of hammers; but no adamant is harder than the stony heart of sinners. This iron heart, then, this stony heart, this heart more than adamantine, the blood of Christ softens, and of his martyrs, who supplied what was lacking in his sufferings. By this proof that supreme shepherd, and, as Peter says, chief of shepherds, testified that he is the good shepherd, because he laid down his life for the sheep, giving us an example, so that we who, each according to our portion, act in his stead, may ourselves be ready to shed our blood for the Lord's flock, unless we would rather appear hirelings than shepherds. The words of the disciple agree with the words of the Lord. For when he had said that he rejoiced in the sufferings by which he completed the sufferings of Christ, himself also enduring for the body of Christ, which is the church, such things as the Lord had suffered, he added the reason why he suffered them gladly: "Of which," he says, "I have been made a minister according to the dispensation of God which was given to me for you, that I may fulfil the word of God." And in another place he writes that he had fully preached the gospel. Just as, therefore, the sufferings of Christ are completed by the deaths of the martyrs, so the promises of Christ are confirmed by the blood of shepherds. For no document is more beyond doubt than one sealed with the blood of so many martyrs. This, surely, is to fulfil the word of God; this is to fill out the gospel.

But meanwhile a most grievous sorrow rises in my mind, beloved, when I reflect that, while that still fresh blood of Christ ought to be seething in the hearts of the faithful, there are so many in whom love has grown cold; and I am tormented the more grievously because the church has not a few such shepherds, who not only do not set their bodies against the attacks of wolves, but even play the wolf themselves, while they slaughter and destroy the souls of the simple, serving their own belly, gain and ambition, and so far from fulfilling the word of God that they rather peddle it and adulterate it with impious doctrines; nor do they reflect that that chief of shepherds will, in a most severe judgement, demand back from their hands each one of the sheep for whose redemption he had shed his blood. But their own punishment awaits them; now it is better that, setting complaints aside, we exhort one another to the duty we owe to Christ.

We have received a threefold witness from Christ; we must render him a threefold witness in return. Let us faithfully hand on the rudiments to those who are to be baptized, and the more perfect things to the baptized. Let us strengthen them with the fruits of the Spirit, calling them on to the heavenly life, and, if the situation demands it, let us gladly spend even our life for the flock entrusted to us, and by our death glorify God in our turn. And lest it seem strange to anyone that God is glorified by the death of men, hear blessed John in the gospel, speaking thus of Peter, to whom the Lord had foretold that when he had grown old, he would be girded by another and led where he did not wish: "signifying by what death he was to glorify God." All, then, who from the founding of the world have died for God, for righteousness and piety, have glorified God by their death. For almsgiving, fasting, prayers and other exercises of piety even hypocrites feign; but no one has eagerly undergone death except one who was firmly persuaded that nothing adverse can befall those who persevere in the love of God.

Yet not everyone who is killed is at once a martyr: assassins and pirates are killed too. It is not the punishment that makes the martyr, but the cause. And if some are read of as having bravely brought death upon themselves, it was either weakness seeking in death an end to pain, or ambition, or madness. Nor is it bearing witness to God to do what both displeases God and is forbidden even by the laws of the nations. There is a very great difference between barbarous savagery and the most modest constancy of the martyrs, weak in itself, strong in Christ. There are those who numb the body by certain arts so as not to feel the torments; in this way, indeed, sorcerers fortify themselves against the hands of executioners. There are also violent passions which take sensation away from the mind, so that men endure even death without fear. But that calm and gentle quality, that humbly sublime and sublimely humble quality, we do not see except in the martyrs of Christ. They do not glare at the executioner with fierce eyes, they do not threaten the tyrant; they grieve more over the blindness of those men than over their own afflictions. Indeed Christ cries out in them too: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." They look at nothing but heaven, where they have laid up all their hope. So the Lord himself was led to the slaughter like a lamb without a voice; and if he uttered any word, it showed a mild and calm spirit more than any silence could have. How gently he addresses Judas the traitor, how calmly he answered when struck with a slap, how he says nothing fierce to Annas and Caiaphas, how tranquilly he answered Pilate. Finally, when the Pharisees, as if victors, wagged their heads, raging against him with the bitterest insults, he, most gentle, cries out: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."

So dying is not in itself witness; but to die in this way is to bear witness to God. Stephen, a young man among murderers, a lamb among wolves, stood with a calm and angelic face and, after the Lord's example, prays for those stoning him, and has his eyes nowhere but on heaven. There he was found worthy to see him by whose protection he was superior to his persecutors. Whoever truly fears God does not dread the cruelties of men. Whoever loves the heavenly life from the heart easily holds his life cheap, and for him, as for blessed Paul, to live is Christ, to die is gain. Or is it not an immense gain to exchange this life, both brief and polluted by countless evils, for everlasting happiness? Here the Lord, as in all other things, showed himself a pattern for us. For when the final act of martyrdom was at hand, which, they say, ought in plays to be the best, he withdrew, threw himself on the ground, [praying] at length and repeatedly, and, drenched in a bloody sweat, displayed in himself the weakness of our nature, having first declared his weariness and sorrow of soul even unto death, so that we should not fall into despair if, when everything threatens imminent death, we feel nature's horror. For if the sense of pain were not present, martyrdom would have nothing admirable about it; but to overcome pain is worthy of a crown. To shudder at death belongs to nature; to conquer nature by strength of mind belongs to grace. Paul can do all things, but in him who strengthens him. But by what defences is the weakness of nature overcome? If we prostrate ourselves wholly on the ground, that is, if we attribute nothing at all to our own strength, if we watch and pray earnestly, if we submit our will to the divine will, and say those words from the soul, with our whole heart: "Let this cup pass, if it can be, but let it be done not as I will, but as you will."

I have known, and wept for, some endowed with great strength of mind, who when already very near the crown failed and denied him whom they had long professed. What was the cause? They had turned their eyes away from him who alone gives strength to the weak; they had broken off prayer and begun to look to human defences. They contemplated the paltry powers of their own nature, they considered the hooks, the claws, the red-hot plates, the sword and fire, and the rest of the torture-chamber's apparatus, dreadful even to behold, and they compared the savagery of the torments with their own strength, and so they let the victory slip from their hands. When someone thinks thus, "This I can endure, that I cannot endure," he will never bring his martyrdom to a happy end. But he who hands himself over wholly to the divine will, looking to nothing but his help, he alone is firm and unconquered. This, however, cannot come about unless there is a true and living faith, hesitating in nothing, inquiring into nothing. Do not consider how great the tyrant's cruelty is, how great man's weakness, but how great is the power of the Lord, who contends and has conquered in his members.

So, to turn back from the digression to what we had set out to do: just as the Lord's death was more powerful than his life, so he willed the death of his martyrs to be powerful. For what is weaker than to be bound, condemned, beaten, tortured, killed, and to offer one's body to the will of the executioner? This sight sometimes moves to pity even the most savage tyrants. But when at the tombs of the martyrs diseases are driven out, demons roar, monarchs are terrified, miracles flash forth, idols fall down, then it appears how effective and powerful the blood of the martyrs is. "His presence is weak, his letters weighty," the most blessed teacher of the gentiles heard said. This too will rightly be applied to the martyrs: life weak and despised, death weighty and powerful. Now, not all martyrs have equal eagerness in torments, just as not all die by the same kind of death. Those three blessed youths found refreshment in the midst of the flames and, enclosed by the harmless element as if in a chamber, sang a hymn to the Lord. Daniel likewise enjoyed the company of lions without harm. Blessed Andrew, as a history, human indeed but of sufficiently approved credit, relates, went to the cross rejoicing and congratulating himself. Others die by degrees in long and varied torments, and yet are not granted to end their pain by death. This too, then, belongs to a true martyr: to commit this also wholly to the will of God. He knows what is expedient for us and what is most conducive to his own glory. Only this must be constantly borne in mind: whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. Nor should anyone be displeased with himself if he feels heavy and prolonged distress in body and mind alike; only let him trust in him for whom he contends. He will not allow anyone to be tempted beyond what he is able, but with the temptation will also make a way out. He sometimes allows certain of the elect to fail in torments, so that they may recognize their weakness, and afterwards makes the same men most valiant in the contest. By this dispensation Peter denied the Lord three times, so that, taught how little he could do by his own strength, he might strengthen his brothers. And how would he strengthen them? So that, distrusting themselves, they might place all their confidence in the Lord.

But now it is time to discourse to your charity on the other kind of martyrdom, which must be discussed even more carefully, because it is hidden and common to all times. For Neros, Diocletians, Deciuses and Maximins do not always rage; yet the devil never ceases to harass those who have professed the military service of Christ. And perhaps, by Christ's gift, there will hereafter be times in which no persecutions by tyrants will afflict the church; yet contests will never be lacking, never martyrdoms by which godly people may glorify God. The church, indeed, still campaigning in this exile, applauds with special rejoicing those who in professing the name of Jesus have faithfully laid down their lives, and people flock with great eagerness to their memorial shrines; but the heavenly theatre, the myriads of angels and the countless people of the righteous reigning with Christ, applaud all who bear witness, by integrity and innocence of life, to the sincere faith and unconquered love they have towards the Lord Jesus.

And God is glorified not only by profession of faith, which according to Paul is made with the mouth unto salvation, but also by confession of wrongs committed. Lest we seem to say this rashly of ourselves, testimonies of the scriptures must be brought forward. Well then, unless the life of the godly redounded to the glory of God, Christ would not say in the gospel: "that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." Nor would the apostle Paul write to the Galatians: "and they glorified God in me." This is confirmed also by the contrary of what we have said. For if the name of God is polluted and dishonoured by the impious life of his people, surely it is honoured by their good life. The apostle also condemns the impious wisdom of the philosophers, who, though they had known God, yet did not glorify him as God. They professed wisdom and displayed the utmost folly. So, though they professed that God exists, yet by living shamefully and sacrificing to idols they in a way obscured the glory of God with false witness, as if he were neither just nor truthful, or as if he were not one but many, or as if he were like stones. This most blessed Paul attests even more plainly, writing to the Corinthians: "You have been bought," he says, "at a great price; glorify and carry God in your body." For this reason God redeemed us at the price of his blood, that, once cleansed from sins, we might thenceforth lead a life worthy of him.

And we bear the emperor's token stamped on our foreheads. What if someone bearing the sign of Christ performs the works of Belial: is not he whose insignia we bear dishonoured? On the other hand, just as an emperor is pleased with a most vigorous soldier, judging that soldier's valour to be an honour and ornament to himself, so God glories in those whom he has redeemed, whom he has washed, whom he has sanctified, whom he has deemed worthy of the bounty of the Spirit, if by holiness of life they have shown that the Lord's grace in them was not in vain. If Paul glories in the godliness of his disciples, calling them his joy and his crown, though he was nothing but the steward of another's gift, does not the Lord glory far more over those for whom he died? Again, when in the book of Job the Lord speaks to Satan in this way: "Have you not noticed my servant Job, how there is none like him on the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from wickedness?", does he not utter the speech of one glorying in his worshipper? And blessed Paul used an even more splendid expression, writing the second epistle to the Corinthians: "But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus, and manifests the fragrance of the knowledge of him through us in every place, for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God." A good name is better than precious ointments. Scripture is accustomed to call glorious fame perfumes. Yet God does not glory after the manner of men, pleased with himself and exulting, but he counts our salvation his glory; and therefore the apostle added: "among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing." How is God glorified in those who are being saved? Because in them his mercy is made illustrious. How in those who are perishing? Because in them his justice is declared.

Now the very course of our discourse has led us to the point of teaching that God is glorified also by the confession of sins. Here at once there meets us, from the book of Joshua son of Nun, Achan, because of whom, since against the divine edict he had taken from what was under the ban a splendid scarlet cloak, two hundred shekels of silver and a tongue of gold of fifty shekels, the people of Israel turned their backs to the enemy. And so Joshua said to Achan: "My son, give glory to the Lord God of Israel, and confess and show me what you have done; do not hide it." Having confessed, he paid the penalty, and the fury of the Lord was turned away. That confession made clear the justice and wisdom of God: his wisdom, because nothing was hidden from his eyes; his justice, because not without cause had he allowed the enemy to prevail against Israel, and because no human being violates his laws with impunity. What Achan had pilfered was nothing great; yet it was a great lesson to the whole people, how dangerous it is to neglect God's commands and to want to deceive him, as if anything escaped him, or as if he favoured transgressors. And he indeed, though he was a Jew, for a single sin which seemed light to him paid the severest penalty, stoned by the whole people, redeeming the salvation of his soul by the destruction of his body. For God does not judge twice for the same thing.

But what punishment awaits those who, after so great a light and grace of the gospel, after they have once been enlightened, have tasted also the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, have tasted likewise the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then slide back into many monstrous crimes, crucifying the Son of God for themselves and holding him up to contempt? They are the more pitiable in this, that being such, they nevertheless spurn the remedy of saving penance, and despise the church offering her motherly bosom and inviting them to the restoration of health. How great a disgrace do you think such a defection brands upon the church? Nor can that disgrace fail to touch Christ, who is the head of the church and counts as his own in every respect whatever belongs to his body and members. On the other hand, how great is the exultation of the whole church when one who has fallen is reconciled to the church through penance! And lest we think this joy exists only among us, let us hear the Lord speaking in the gospel according to Luke: "So I tell you, there will be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous who do not need penance." For this sentence ends the parable of the shepherd who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep, sought with much labour the one that had strayed from the flock, and when at last he found it, laid it on his shoulders and restored it to the fold. With a similar sentence he closes the parable of the woman who had found the lost drachma: "So I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner doing penance." Yet this is not to be taken as though it were more pleasing to God and his angels to return to godliness after a fall than to persevere in innocence without a fall; but Scripture speaks in its own way according to human feelings, wishing to testify that the conversion of sinners is most pleasing to God. For he does not seek the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live.

And sometimes the falls of godly people, however enormous, are turned by divine dispensation to the highest benefit of the church. So fell the chief of the apostles, so Paul the teacher of the gentiles, so Mary Magdalene, in whom the church now especially glories, and whose falls turned out to the strengthening and comfort of the house of God. Moreover, he is not speaking here of the truly righteous, but of Pharisaic righteousness, as he says elsewhere: "Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill." But those to whom the Lord said this were not healthy; rather, puffed up by some sort of observance of the law, they seemed to themselves healthy, and therefore did not desire a physician.

Since these things are so, beloved brother, let us strive by constant exhortations to rouse the minds of the faithful, so that with their whole life also they may render martyrdom, that is, witness, to God. This is so far from being something to neglect that, unless it has gone before, the martyrdom borne in blood is not martyrdom. For in vain will you offer your neck to the executioner unless you have first put to death your members which are on earth, that is, the passions which war against the spirit: hatred, envy, avarice, lust. Whoever serves these has in a way denied God, and while professing Christ with his mouth, confesses Satan as God with his life. Nor should this saying seem too harsh to anyone, since it is true and salutary: whatever any man puts before God, he makes a god for himself, and we cannot serve two masters; for there is one God, to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, the whole strength.

Whoever, then, says with his mouth, "I believe in one God," and serves avarice or lust or luxury, lies to himself and contradicts himself, sounding one thing with his tongue and hiding another in his mind, bearing witness to God with his voice only, while his life worships Satan. But the witness of life is more effective than that of the tongue. Not everyone who says "Lord, Lord" will enter the kingdom, but he who does the will of the heavenly Father. Works too have their own tongue, have their own eloquence, even when the tongue is silent. Therefore the Lord speaks thus in the gospel of John: "The works which the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works which I do, bear witness about me." Just as good works, then, profess God, so bad ones in a way say: "There is no God, nor knowledge in the Most High." Who would not tremble, who would not shudder, who would not tear his garments, who would not stop his ears, if he heard such words from a Christian? How great a horror, how great a grief seizes our minds when someone, overcome by torments and ordered to deny Christ, denies him and burns incense before the statue of Jupiter! How we tremble, fearing that God in anger may hurl the thunderbolt of his wrath at us, that the earth may gape and swallow us up! For sometimes the impiety of one man involves many in a shared punishment; and there are crimes so monstrous that even to have seen or heard them is abominable. But why are we elsewhere so indulgent towards a like crime? Why do we flatter both ourselves and others so much? But see what the apostle says of such people, writing to Titus: "They profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds." The same, in the first [epistle] to Timothy, of the widow who neglects her household: "But if anyone does not take care of her own, and especially of her household, she has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever." If she who is rather negligent of her household has denied the faith, what do you think he would say of those who have given themselves wholly to mammon and the belly? Paul is certainly speaking of Christians when, writing to the Philippians, he says: "whose end is destruction, whose god is the belly." He censures the same people writing to the Romans: "Such people do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly." He said "feel" for "worship," according to the custom of the Scriptures. They worship the belly whom they hold as God. Further, on avarice he pronounces even more plainly, writing to the Colossians: "Put to death," he says, "your members which are on earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols."

We curse those who prostrate themselves before the image of Diana: how much more justly do we curse those who serve mammon with their whole heart, who sacrifice to it every day? And if the avaricious man who is held fast by the pursuit of money is an idolater, he who hoards what has come to him by inheritance or been gained by industry and does not pay it out to the needy, what must we judge of those who pile up wealth by pimping, by usury, by robbery, by fraud, by false accusations, by oppressing the poor? And this service of idols is found not only among Christians but, what is to be lamented, even among bishops. Further, drunkenness is so common in our Africa that they almost do not count it a crime. Do we not see, at the memorials of the martyrs, a Christian forced into drunkenness by a Christian? Or do we think this a lighter crime than to sacrifice a goat to Bacchus? To me it seems much graver, if we are willing to weigh the matter by right reason. When the tyrant says, 'Deny Christ and sacrifice to Jupiter, and be our friend, or die,' often the tongue denies while the heart protests, and the hand burns incense while the mind within adores Christ. Although this too is a most grave crime, yet the weakness of human nature lightens somewhat the guilt of impiety. There Satan speaks to you through the voice of the tyrant; but what does the same one say to you through your own desire? 'Deny Christ, and be rich: sacrifice to Mammon and send Christ his notice of dismissal.' What is it that he promises? Gold and silver, useless matter unless you put it to use. Nor does he say, 'Die,' but 'Delight your eyes'; or rather he says this: 'Gain money which you will have for a short time, and lose your soul for eternity.' And yet here you willingly bend your knees to Satan and, having denied Christ, hand yourself over wholly to him as his property. But what does Christ [say]? 'Be mine and live for eternity: despise these temporary riches, and I will repay you a hundredfold in this age, and eternal life in the age to come. Leave the earth and receive heaven.' And God, promising these things, is deserted, and the devil, promising things of so little worth, and promising them falsely, is adored. O foul defection! O shameful idolatry! O unjust exchange! With what reward did he entice the first founders of the human race? He showed an apple and gave death. He deceived them with a lie: 'You will not die, but you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.' And they, deluded, what a Lord did they desert, and to whom did they defect? From what happiness did they fall, and into what miseries did they throw themselves? But that same prince of darkness who spoke to Eve through the serpent speaks to us through his henchmen and ministers, through bawds and pimps, through those who lure us to the love of money, to ambition, to pleasure, calling us away from the sincerity which is in Christ Jesus. The same one speaks to us through our desires which live in our members. Nor does he say what a human tyrant says, 'Either obey me or die,' nor does he display prisons, chains, hooks, frying pans or blazing furnaces, not crosses, nooses or swords, but only: 'Despise God, renounce the inheritance of heavenly life, and commit adultery, and you will get pleasure.' But what kind? Momentary, and of the body only; and seasoned with how many bitternesses? With disgrace, with danger, and above all with the secret torment of conscience. This is the devil's bait, this his enlistment bounty. And what kind of pay is it? Let the blessed apostle say it, with greater authority: 'The wages of sin is death.' What death? That of the body, which alone a human tyrant threatens and can inflict? No, but the death of Gehenna, which knows no end. The human tyrant has more power than the devil. The former in a way coerces human nature; the latter can do nothing but entice: he cannot throw you down unless you consent; to have despised him is to have conquered.

Greater pardon, therefore, is owed to one who denies Christ under torture than to one who willingly assents to the devil, to have believed whom is to have denied Christ. He is a liar and the father of every lie, and his promises, however flattering their face, are nothing but illusions luring to destruction. So let no one flatter himself thus: 'I am a sinner, I love money, I serve lust, I strive after honours, I indulge in revenge, I am given over to pleasures: but I have not denied Christ.' But the Lord himself cries out against you: 'You cannot worship two masters.' And meanwhile you shudder at the abominable name of *turificatus* [one who has offered incense to idols] or *libellatus* [one who has obtained a certificate of sacrifice], though you yourself are perhaps worse than the *turificati* or *libellati*. A human fear too violent for human nature to overcome drove them to utter impious words with their tongue while their conscience protested; you, enticed by so cheap a petty wage, willingly defect to him from whose tyranny Christ redeemed you with his blood, to whom you have now wholly come to belong, as the apostle says: 'You were bought at a great price, and now you are not your own.' You professed his service at the saving bath, you gave him your name, you were initiated in his sacraments, you received the donative and the pledge of the Spirit, so that you might have no doubt of the promised pay; and at the same time you declared perpetual enmity to the devil, you renounced all his pomps and pleasures, you blew him away, you hissed him off, you swore the oath in the words of the Redeemer: and while you serve so many vices, you are pleased with yourself because you are not yet a *turificatus* or *libellatus*.

If some soldier who had sworn the oath in Caesar's words fled to the Turk and, at his will, did things he knew to be most displeasing to Caesar, would he not, when caught, be hauled off to punishment as a deserter, as an oath-breaker, as a runaway? And who would listen to him defending himself thus: 'I am not a deserter, I have not denied Caesar'? Would he not at once hear: 'What does it matter if your tongue was silent? In very fact you denied him, and more than denied him, since you not only deserted your service but even went over to the tyrant, the irreconcilable enemy of your emperor'? Rightly the ears of the faithful abhor the word 'apostate'; but this is to be cursed not only where the profession of the name of Christ is renounced by burning a bit of incense or by a written certificate, but wherever the laws of Christ are despised and Satan is obeyed. For it does not matter what the tongue says: if it says 'Christ' while the mind is given over to crimes, it is not profession but hypocrisy, which would deny Christ if the fear pressed it that presses the *turificati* or *libellati*. And in those things which so fight with one another that neither tolerates the company of the other, whenever we embrace the one we have disowned the other, whenever we reject the one we acknowledge the other. Such are light and darkness, war and peace, death and life, God and Belial, as blessed Paul too testifies in the second [epistle] to the Corinthians: 'For what participation has righteousness with iniquity, or what fellowship has light with darkness? And what agreement has Christ with Belial?' To have cleaved to Belial is to have denied Christ, [even if] you profess Christ with your tongue or your dress.

If any of the simpler folk doubts this, I will give a crude and evident proof. Let us imagine a tyrant speaking thus to a Christian: 'You will burn incense to Jupiter,' adding nothing and not demanding that he deny Christ. If he burns it, will it not be plain to all that he has denied Christ by this very act, that he has offered incense to Jupiter, even if he utters nothing impious against Christ? Just as those who use magic arts (from which evil the Lord's mercy has freed us, as from all the others in which we were once held when we walked according to the old man) tacitly deny Christ, while they have a pact with demons. Further, if the Maccabean brothers together with their mother preferred to be killed by so many tortures rather than eat pork, judging thus that whoever knowingly and willingly violates the precepts of the law denies God, the author of the law, how do they flatter themselves who grow old in luxury, drunkenness, avarice, robberies, adulteries and other crimes which even the laws of the gentiles refused to leave unpunished? And though they deny Christ in so many ways, though they sacrifice to demons so often, do they demand to be counted as Christians? And among them are some who commit these things openly and almost even glory in the worst deeds, so far are they from shame or regret for what they have done. And yet they dare to come into the church of the saints, they dare to mingle with the Lord's flock. Such people the church sometimes tolerates, lest, provoked, they disturb the people of God even more; but what does it profit not to be cast out of the assembly of the godly, if you have deserved to be cast out? For to be cast out is a remedy and a step towards recovering health; to have deserved expulsion is the height of evils. And in vain does one mingle with the assembly of the saints in a temple made with hands, if he has been removed from fellowship with God and from the whole mystical body of Christ.

We must also consider how greatly Christians shrink from things sacrificed to idols, from entering shrines, and even from the images themselves. Though blessed Paul proclaims that neither an idol is anything nor a thing sacrificed to an idol, much less is a shrine built of stones anything; and yet the minds of very many are held by such scruple that they would sooner meet death than taste what has been sacrificed to idols, and they count it an inexpiable sacrilege if they enter a shrine of Jupiter or Apollo or Diana, and think themselves gravely defiled by touching an image. For my part I approve the scruple of such people, if it is consistent in all things. As it is, alas, one may see some almost superstitiously fearful in these matters, and in others, where there was weightier cause for fear, all too unconcerned. Of itself the touch of an idol does not stain the soul, nor entering a shrine, nor eating what was sacrificed to an idol; but of itself love of money, incest, robbery, hypocrisy and monsters like these pollute the conscience. How consistent is it to shudder at entering a shrine, and not to shudder at sacrificing victims to demons in a temple consecrated to the Holy Spirit? Saint Paul cries out, writing to the Corinthians: 'Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you? But if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.' Again in the same epistle: 'Or do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own?' But if God has consecrated the hearts of Christians to himself so as to dwell in them through his Spirit, there he takes his delight and walks about, there he loves a pure victim to be offered to him in every place. And does he who, having driven out the Holy Spirit, brings into this temple sacred to God the abominations which Ezekiel beheld in his mystic vision, who makes there a seat for Mammon, Venus, Comus, Bacchus and other monsters, who sacrifices there the foulest victims to demons, fear to enter a shrine of the gentiles lest he be defiled? So let no one flatter himself in vain; God is not mocked. Let our religion be consistent, and let us not curse others while we ourselves are liable to graver crimes; nor let us be scrupulously timid in one place and shamelessly impious in another. But having once professed Christ, let us render him witness with our whole life, and glorify him on every side by obeying his precepts, so that by this people may know that we truly trust in him, that we love him from the heart, and that it was not in pretence that at the sacred bath we pledged ourselves to his service.

The blessed apostle foretold that persecution would not be lacking to anyone who wishes to live godly in Christ Jesus. If there is no tyrant, no torturer, no plunderer, concupiscence will not be lacking, which offers us daily matter for martyrdom. Finally, these very evils which the life of mortals brings with it, and which the godly share with the ungodly, will prepare for us the crown of martyrdom if we bear them calmly and with thanksgiving. Nor are all those who were not finished off by a violent death deprived of the glory of martyrdom. Who would dare to remove from the number of the martyrs either the patriarch Abraham, or his son Isaac, or blessed Job? What torture-chambers have racked the body more severely than the affections of nature racked the patriarch's mind, when without hesitation, at God's command, he prepared to sacrifice his only son, uniquely dear, in whom lay all his hope of posterity? What did Isaac lack for martyrdom, who without a murmur allowed himself to be bound and laid on the pyre, and did not take fright at the sword swung at his neck? And whose martyrdom shall we dare to compare with what Job suffered?

But if anyone still distrusts our words, he certainly cannot distrust the words of blessed Paul. Writing to the Hebrews, he begins from Abel and goes through to Gideon, reviewing a huge catalogue of saints, among whom more did not die by a violent death; indeed few are those who died so. And yet he declares of them all: 'And these were found approved by the witness of faith', clearly declaring that the martyrdom of faith is also accomplished by a good life. The usage of the church indeed distinguishes them by titles, calling martyrs those who died by a violent death, and confessors those who steadfastly, amid tortures and threats of death, professed the name of the Lord Jesus, ready to meet death, or rather seeking the supreme crown of martyrdom. Before God, however, all who have crucified their flesh with its vices and concupiscences, all who have truly died with Christ and been buried with him in baptism, so that they no longer live for themselves nor for the world to which they have once died, but for him who died for them, are martyrs and will not be cheated of the martyrs' crown; and above all monks who are truly monks and virgins who are truly virgins. For neither a deserted place, sackcloth for clothing, pulse for food, nor fasts nor sleeping on the ground make a complete monk; under these wrappings there sometimes lurks a very worldly mind. This is detected if they are called to some office in the church: there you may see some of them very easily overcome by pleasures, more impatient of injuries, more eager for revenge than anyone else from among the common people. What is the reason? Because they have exercised the body more than the mind, although blessed Paul teaches that bodily exercise is of little use, while godliness avails for all things.

I would not say this because those who chastise their body in such ways and bring it into subjection are to be disapproved, but because Satan, equipped with a thousand arts, sometimes deludes the unwary, transforming himself into an angel of light, and from such exercises of the body induces in them a false conviction of holiness; and while inwardly they are soaked in spiritual vices, they are held godly both by themselves and by others. Such was the righteousness of the Pharisees, to which, with Christ as judge, the unrighteousness of the publican was preferred. So too are the foolish virgins, who think it solid godliness to have a body untouched by a man, when the mind is utterly corrupted by avarice, pride, envy and detraction. There are also false widows, who while they live in pleasures are dead to Christ. In sum, however, everyone who is truly a Christian, of whatever state or order, has his own contests, has his own cross; if he takes it up patiently, if he bears it steadfastly, he glorifies the Lord by his witness, provided only that he does not claim for himself the praise of good works; for this is not to glorify God but to make oneself illustrious.

Each of the faithful has his own contests, has the devil as adversary, has God as *agonothetes* [president of the games], has as theatre not only the church and the angels but also the unbelievers, as Paul says to the Corinthians: 'We have been made a spectacle to the world, and to angels and to men.' If we win, the angels glory, the churches of the faithful glory, and Christ himself glories in his members. But if we are beaten through our cowardice, Satan triumphs with his angels, the unbelievers mock us and heap insults on God, saying: 'Look, those who boast that they have been redeemed from the tyranny of Satan, who proclaim that they are dead to the world, are no less beaten by their desires than we are, whom they say are still held under the reign of Satan. What use to them is baptism, in which they say the old man is put off with his deeds and the new one put on, who is created according to God? What use to them is the Holy Spirit, by whose will they say they are governed? Why do they always have the gospel in their mouth, when their whole life is at odds with the precepts of the gospel?' With what shame, do you think, is the church covered when these things are thrown at it by enemies and it has nothing with which to refute the reproaches? Do we not see the whole assembly of the church lower its eyes and blush whenever some virgin who had married Christ slips from the angelic company and falls away to debauchery or marriage? What grief fills the minds of all of us, but especially of the shepherds, if ever a soldier of Christ, worsted by torments, has renounced his emperor? And how great, on the other side, is Satan's triumph?

Therefore, dearest brothers, if we truly love God, if daily we ask from the heart 'hallowed be your name', let us watch with the utmost zeal that we never defile his name, but glorify him both by death and by life, living according to blessed Paul's admonitions without complaint, as simple children of God, without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom we may shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life to the glory of Christ Jesus, our king and *agonothetes*, who counts as his own whatever is done in his members. Let us suffer with him, that we may be glorified with him on the day of the Lord. Let us make him illustrious here before men, that he may make us illustrious with his glory before his angels when, as blessed Paul says, he comes to be glorified in his saints. No one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully. And those who seek a corruptible crown abstain from all things, leaving nothing undone that leads to victory: what is it fitting for us to do, that we may attain that incorruptible and unfading crown of immortal life in heaven?

Here, if anyone asks how someone can be a martyr without the shedding of blood: whoever follows righteousness with such a mind that he would sooner accept death than be willing to turn aside from righteousness, his ready will shall be counted to him as martyrdom. For God judges no one by the outcome of events but by the disposition. Why should he be cheated of the glory of martyrdom through whom it did not stand that he did not accomplish martyrdom? Just as, conversely, whoever lives with such a mind that he would deny Christ if loss of goods or torture of the body or death had to be accepted will receive the wages of an apostate. Will he who perjures himself for a little money fear to deny Christ if his whole property is endangered, if infamy, prison and death are threatened? Will he who for a slight fever flees to the remedies of enchantresses prefer to endure tortures grimmer than death rather than renounce Christ? Indeed, will he who so often falls away from Christ for a brief little pleasure of the flesh, for momentary glory, hold his life cheap for Christ? It was not the tyrant who made this man an apostate; rather he came to the tyrant an apostate. And as the manner of fighting is similar, so the minds of the brothers are to be fortified for these battles with the same arms with which we have shown they are to be strengthened for martyrdom. It is faith that fights and conquers in the martyrs, and no one has failed in torments except through failure of faith.

God must therefore be prayed to constantly to increase faith in us, for it is God's gift and to him is owed all the glory of victory. Let us press upon their minds and fix in them how horrible a crime all idolatry is, how severely it was punished by God under the old law, how many thousands Moses slaughtered on account of the golden calf. Then let a comparison be set out between open idolatry, when sacrifice is made to images, and hidden idolatry, when God is despised and Satan is obeyed through concupiscence. Then let God, the fount of all good, and the devil, the prince of all wickedness, be compared with each other. Let the inequality of the company also be shown: on the one side are the children of God, fellow citizens of the angels and heirs of blessed immortality; on the other the children of Belial, the fellowship of all the demons and heirs of Gehenna. Let the unequal kind of service also be compared, and the differing wages set side by side. If these things have first been made convincing and fixed in the inmost heart, victory will be easy. As it is, faith floats on many lips, while in the heart it is either nothing or extremely feeble. For who does not profess what we read in Deuteronomy: 'Hear: the Lord your God is one Lord'? And: 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve'? Who does not daily recite with his mouth 'I believe in God the Father almighty'? But he does not believe in God who does not place in him alone the confidence of all his happiness; nor does he have one God and Lord who through fornication, through luxury and avarice, does Satan's bidding; nor does he serve him alone who serves his belly, who is given over to this world, which lies in wickedness.

The heathen think there are many gods, and do you think yourself a perfect Christian because you are convinced that there is one God? What great thing are you doing? The Jews believe the same, who blaspheme daily in their synagogues; the demons believe the same, and tremble. If you truly believe in God, believe him just and truthful: just in rewarding the godly and punishing the ungodly, truthful in his promises. Believe that there is no hope of salvation except through his Son, whom he handed over to death for us all; believe that no evil can befall those who have handed themselves wholly over to his will and persevere in him. This is to believe in God the Father, this is to believe in his Son, this is to believe in the Holy Spirit, one God, and in the holy Church, the mystical body of Christ, outside which there is no salvation and in which there is no destruction.

Whoever has fixed the feet of his mind on such a rock will stand unmoved against every onset of temptations. For example: you have been provoked by abuse, and the flesh suggests to you a desire for revenge. Before you answer, think this over with yourself: 'The devil has put this abusive man up to it, to throw me down and, once thrown down, to destroy me; but listen to what your commander, under whom you serve, advises: Blessed, he says, are the meek, for they shall possess the earth; and: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay. [Listen to] what that bravest captain of Christ, Paul, advises: Not avenging ourselves, dearly beloved, but give place to wrath.' The devil says: 'Enjoy revenge and lose eternal life.' God says: 'Overcome evil with good, and do not resist evil, and receive with my Son the possession of the heavenly kingdom.' Then consider which of the two it is better to obey. The devil says to you through your lust: 'Commit adultery and enjoy the passing pleasure of the body, and be my slave and co-heir of Gehenna.' Listen rather to what God says to you: 'Spurn passing pleasure and receive a hundredfold joy of a good conscience in this age and eternal life in the age to come', and weigh which of the two should rather be heeded. Satan suggests to you through the feeling of the flesh, as through Eve, 'Live merrily'; on the other side Christ says: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall receive comfort. In the same way, concerning the other temptations, hold up against the tempter the shield of the Scriptures, in which God speaks to you with no less faithfulness than if he were speaking to you in person, mouth to mouth. From these torrents take stones for yourself with which to throw down the proud Goliath. You have the example from your Lord: so he laid the devil low. And do not lose heart if he attacks more often and then comes at you with greater engines: he can do nothing against him who is with you. Say that saying of John: Greater is he who is in us than he who is in this world. Let that saying of the Lord come to mind: Have confidence, for I have overcome the world. If a soldier of Christ has been trained for the conflict with these speeches, he will find his adversary weaker day by day.

Yet the watches must not be relaxed whenever the enemy feigns calm; rather, watching for his ambushes, let him say with blessed Habakkuk: I will stand upon my watch and fix my step upon the rock, keeping my heart with all vigilance, so that no access lies open to him who prowls about seeking whom he may devour. Now the safest defence of the heart is sobriety, with urgent prayer and constant meditation on the Scriptures. For all Scripture inspired by God is profitable for teaching, for reproving, for correcting, for instructing in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work. From it, therefore, sayings are to be gathered which you may have at hand and as it were girded for battle, so that with them you may at once throw down the serpent as he raises his head. For there is no disease of the soul for which divine Scripture would not supply a ready remedy. From here are to be gathered the examples of the godly, but above all of Christ, by which each may either encourage or console himself.

I come now to those evils which either accompany human nature itself or seem to be inflicted by chance. These too a godly mind, trained for fighting, will turn into material for its crown. I will make what I say clearer by an example. Someone is stripped of his means, whether by war or shipwreck or robbery. Let him not at once think of the noose or of a way to make good by evil arts what has been lost, but let him speak thus with himself: 'It is the Lord who is testing me, whether I love him with my whole heart. He gave, he has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.' Let him give thanks that he received [it] from the Lord's kindness; let him give thanks that he lost [it] for the testing of his faith. If he says this in the spirit in which holy Job said it, he will receive the reward with him. The Lord weighs not how much someone loses but how patiently, just as he does not regard how much someone gives to the needy but in what spirit. Someone has a son uniquely dear: premature death bereaves you of him; pestilence robs you of those dearest to you, wife, children, friends: bear it patiently and say: 'So it seemed good to the Lord, and so perhaps it was expedient both for us and for ours. Blessed be the name of the Lord.' There are also diseases which bring tortures no less savage than any cruelty of torturers can inflict, such as pleurisy, sciatica, gout, paralysis, the stone, ulceration of the kidneys and bladder. If anything of this kind befalls, let not the mind be provoked to impatience, let not the tongue break out in blasphemous words, but let it say with blessed David and Eli the priest: It is the Lord; let him do what is good in his eyes. Thus the evils which are not inflicted for the profession of Christ we shall turn into a crown for ourselves and glory for Christ. And perhaps it will come about that the Lord, appeased by our endurance, either takes away the afflictions or lightens them; but if this does not happen, we shall nonetheless by this means bring it about that what would have been unbearable to an impatient mind becomes milder through patience. With these and similar arguments we shall not cease to exhort one another to make illustrious the glory of the Lord, whose title and insignia we bear. Let us render him martyrdom, each in his own state and rank, not only in adversity but also in prosperity. In adversity let us recognise the love of a father who scourges us for correction, and let us give thanks for the charity with which he loves us as sons, whom he does not wish to disown but to receive back amended. In prosperity let us equally give thanks to his goodness, with which he consoles us so that we may bear the weight of temptations. So it will come about that our whole life will be nothing other than a witness, declaring among believers and unbelievers the wisdom, goodness, mercy and truth of God the Father and of his Son Jesus and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.
